object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A business entity from which the organization procures goods, services, or materials. Identified uniquely by vendor number and tracked through onboarding, review, and active usage cycles.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master... Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
It's the thing we quote in every conversation with AP... It's the primary key. It's been the primary key since before I got here.

object_types.name: VendorNumber
object_types.definition: The unique system-generated identifier assigned to each vendor record upon creation.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created... It's the primary key.

object_types.name: LegalName
object_types.definition: The official registered business name of the vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address... By name, usually.

object_types.name: TaxID
object_types.definition: The tax identification number or equivalent for the vendor. Not a unique identifier due to multi-entity organizational structures and duplicate records.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID... We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

object_types.name: VendorStatus
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of a vendor record. Every vendor is in exactly one status at any time.

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended... It defaults to draft the moment the record is created.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: The procurement spend classification of a vendor, indicating the scale of financial commitment and relationship intensity. Every vendor has a spend tier.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold... Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.
Every vendor gets a spend tier. Bronze by default if nobody's assessed them.

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: The compliance risk classification of a vendor, based on the completed risk review. Indicates the level of organizational risk posed by the vendor's operations, data access, geography, and supplier concentration.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high... And I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review -- what data they touch, what geography they operate in, whether they're a sole source.

object_types.name: RiskReview
object_types.definition: A compliance risk assessment and approval record for a vendor. Each review is independently recorded with reviewer identity and date for audit purposes. Multiple reviews accumulate over a vendor's life, but only one current review is active at any time.

source_references.excerpt: Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review. Not zero, and the one has to be signed off... A vendor can have several reviews over its life -- we re-review on a cycle, and every re-review is a new record, we don't edit the old one.
The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: ReviewID
object_types.definition: The unique system-generated identifier for a risk review record.

source_references.excerpt: It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: Contact
object_types.definition: A primary business contact for a vendor within a specific geographic region. Each vendor-region combination has at most one primary contact.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number... Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region.

object_types.name: RegionCode

source_references.excerpt: A purchase order has a PO number. That's its identifier, same idea as vendor number... You can't create one without picking a vendor.

ambiguities.description: Identification of Contact records: The Contact entity has a reference_mode of 'contact_id', but the transcript does not explain how contacts are identified in the system beyond their relationship to a specific Vendor-Region combination. It is unclear whether ContactID is a system-generated surrogate key, or whether the combination of Vendor + Region + ContactName together form the natural key. The system description at line 163 indicates uniqueness is enforced on the Vendor-Region combination, but does not clarify the contact's own identifier scheme.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact... A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact. You cannot have two people both flagged primary for the same vendor in the same region -- the system rejects the second one.

ambiguities.description: Addresses on Vendor records: Dana mentions 'we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one' but the subsequent discussion focuses on legal name, tax ID, and status. The three address types are mentioned as part of onboarding but are not modeled as separate facts. It is unclear whether these should be captured as separate address types within the model, as a single composite address value, or left out of this iteration. The facilitator's scope (lines 237, 279) focuses on vendor, number, amount, and date for POs, suggesting addresses may be deferred.

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Risk Tier optionality and assignment: The constraint that RiskTier is set by a RiskReview (line 291) means a Vendor without a review has no RiskTier. However, the model currently does not capture the inverse: a RiskReview may assign a risk tier, but the exact mechanism by which a Review's outcome maps to a RiskTier value is not explicitly stated. Is RiskTier determined by and stored on the Review, or is it independently assigned? The transcript indicates Raj (Compliance) sets risk tier through the review process, but the cardinality and direction of the fact 'Vendor has RiskTier' versus 'RiskReview assigns RiskTier' is not clarified.

source_references.excerpt: Risk tier comes from the review, so a vendor without a review has no risk tier... A vendor with no review has no risk tier.

ambiguities.description: Status and Purchase Order blocking: The transcript describes a control that 'you can't create one [PO] without picking a vendor' (line 231) and the facilitator states 'you can't raise one against a vendor who isn't active' (line 243). However, the exact mechanism is not specified: does the system prevent PO creation if the vendor status is Draft or Suspended, or is this a procedural gate? Raj later notes (line 251) that what happens to in-flight POs when a vendor is suspended is 'undecided' and the model should not presume post-suspension behavior. The model captures the creation-time control but does not formally constrain POs to Active vendors only, because the enforcement mechanism and scope of applicability remain ambiguous.

source_references.excerpt: You can't create one without picking a vendor... you can't raise one against a vendor who isn't active.
Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Spend Tier default assignment and initial value: Dana states 'Every vendor gets a spend tier. Bronze by default if nobody's assessed them' (line 285-286), indicating Bronze is the default on creation. However, the model does not capture whether this is a rule to enforce (a mandatory constraint with a default value) or merely observational. Is Bronze the only allowed default, or can initial spend tier be set to any of the three values? This affects whether the constraint should be 'Every Vendor has a SpendTier' (which is captured) or additionally 'a newly created Vendor has SpendTier of Bronze.'

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor gets a spend tier. Bronze by default if nobody's assessed them.

ambiguities.description: Vendor-Region-Contact relationship and emptiness: Mei states 'If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only' (line 167). This indicates that a Vendor-Region pair may not have a Contact record if the vendor does not operate in that region. The ternary fact type 'Vendor operates in Region with Contact' implicitly assumes that participation is optional at the Region level (i.e., a vendor may have no contact for a region where it does not operate). However, the model does not capture a separate 'Vendor operates in Region' fact without contact information. The presence or absence of a contact should be inferred from the vendor's operational scope, but that scope is not explicitly modeled.

source_references.excerpt: And can a vendor have no contact in a region?... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only.

ambiguities.description: Tax ID uniqueness and data quality: The facilitator confirms tax ID is 'not an identifier, vendor number is' (line 49). Dana explains duplicates exist because of parent-subsidiary structures filing together, or accidental double onboarding (line 45). The model captures this as a non-unique attribute. However, the business question remains: should duplicates be treated as a constraint violation (and cleaned up), or is the 'same tax ID with different legal entities' scenario a legitimate, allowed state? Mei notes (line 47) that a cleanup project has been on the roadmap for two years, implying duplicates are known but not yet formally resolved in policy.

source_references.excerpt: Could you identify a vendor by tax ID instead?... You'd think so, but no... Noted, but out of scope for today. Tax ID isn't an identifier, vendor number is.

ambiguities.description: Multiple reviews and current-review designation: Raj clarifies that 'A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one' (line 109). The model captures that each Review belongs to exactly one Vendor and that every active Vendor must undergo at least one review. However, the model does not explicitly represent which review is 'current' or 'signed-off.' A constraint such as 'at most one Review per Vendor is marked current' is implied but not formally modeled. The fact type 'Vendor undergoes RiskReview' does not distinguish between historical reviews and the current active review.

source_references.excerpt: A vendor can have several reviews over its life... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one.

ambiguities.description: Region expansion and fixed set: Mei states 'Four regions, fixed?' and the facilitator responds 'Four today. There's been talk of splitting EMEA but it hasn't happened' (line 187). The value constraint on RegionCode is currently set to the four values ['EMEA', 'APAC', 'NA', 'LATAM'], but this is implicitly time-dependent. If EMEA is split in the future, the constraint would need revision. The model captures the current state but does not reflect that region definitions may evolve.

source_references.excerpt: Four regions, fixed?... Four today. There's been talk of splitting EMEA but it hasn't happened.

ambiguities.description: Spend Tier and Risk Tier independence: The facilitator and Mei establish that spend tier (Bronze, Silver, Gold) and risk tier (Low, Medium, High) are independent fields (line 145-147), and a vendor can be 'gold and high at the same time' (line 147). The model correctly captures both as separate attributes on Vendor. However, the business rules around which combinations are allowed or preferred are not discussed. For example, it is not stated whether every combination is valid or if some combinations are excluded (e.g., is a Bronze vendor with High risk possible?). The model assumes all combinations are allowed.

source_references.excerpt: I want to come back to this because I don't think we've finished it... Can a vendor be gold and high at the same time?... Most of our cloud providers are exactly that. Big spend, high risk.
